newsitem.title: USA: Moths can become resistant to transgenic cotton.
newsitem.headline: Moths can become resistant to transgenic cotton.

text.p: Scientists said Monday it could take 10 years for a cotton-eating moth to become resistant to natural toxins bred into transgenic cotton but some pests could show resistance in three years.
The report by entomologist Fred Gould of North Carolina State University appears in the April 15 edition of the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

His five-year study, conducted with colleagues at the U.S. Agriculture Department and Clemson University, studied 2,000 individually mated moth couples and two generations of their offspring. They found that 1.5 of every 1,000 moths carry a copy of a gene for resistance to BT toxins. BT -- Bacillus thuringiensis -- is a soil bacterium.
"Theoretical estimates in the past put the initial frequenc as low as one in a million. Our figure is much higher," Gould said.

The scientists determined that it should take about 10 years for reistance to emerge in Heliothis virescens, a cotton-eating moth. But some pests could become resistant to BT cotton in three to four years, Gould said.
Last year, 1.8 million acres of transgenic BT cotton marketed by Monsanto were planted in the southeastern U.S. with the approval of the Environmental Protection Agency and USDA.
